title: Discovering the Relation Between Architectural Models and Reference Architectures
comment: Accepted at the 49th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE 2027). 13 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. \c{opyright} 2027 IEEE
summary: Assessing whether concrete software architectures are consistent with their reference architecture (RA) is essential to ensure that architectural decisions scale coherently across projects, preserving the quality attributes the RA was designed to guarantee. In the absence of dedicated techniques, mapping the components of an architectural model onto a predefined RA can be addressed only with general-purpose model-comparison algorithms. Our experiments show that these algorithms are inaccurate when applied to RAs. To address this gap, we propose Reference Architecture Mapping Discovery (RAMD), an LLM-based workflow that combines model analysis with structured prompting, and refines results through an iterative RA compliance-checking mechanism. We evaluate RAMD on 64 open-source architectural models spanning three RAs from the IoT, self-driving, and smart parking domains. With domain knowledge and GPT-4o, RAMD reaches 85.8% mapping accuracy and outperforms the strongest baseline by 44.6 percentage points, while ensuring structural consistency with the RA.

title: Understanding Suggested Edits in Stack Overflow: A Large-Scale Empirical Study and Review Prioritization Framework
summary: Suggested edits allow low-reputation users to improve Stack Overflow posts and contribute to the platform's knowledge base. However, we still know little about why these edits are accepted or rejected and how reviewers can efficiently identify problematic edits. In this study, we analyze 3,888,805 suggested edits submitted between 2011 and May 2023. First, we compare accepted and rejected edits using 35 features. We find significant differences between them, with the largest differences related to users' editing history. Second, we manually analyze rejected edits and identify 17 fine-grained rejection reasons. These reasons provide a more detailed understanding of why edits are rejected than Stack Overflow's predefined rejection reasons. Third, we evaluate three models for prioritizing edits based on their likelihood of rejection. The Feature Model, built using the 35 studied features, provides the best trade-off between review rate and rejected-edit recall. At a decision threshold of $τ= 0.40$, it prioritizes 52.3% of edits for human review while capturing 80.8% of rejected edits. In comparison, the Embedding Model captures 78.8% of rejected edits while prioritizing 60.9% of edits, and the EditEx Model captures 72.5% while prioritizing 59.0%. We also conduct a complementary zero-shot evaluation on a separate set of 500 edits. The Feature Model achieves 78.0% recall at $τ= 0.40$, compared with 23.6%-31.2% for GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-32B, and Llama-3.3-70B. Overall, our findings provide a detailed understanding of suggested-edit rejection and show that rejection-risk prediction can help prioritize potentially problematic edits for human review.

title: Structure-Aware Quantum Circuit Equivalence Checking via Sparse Pauli Propagation
summary: Quantum circuit equivalence checking is essential for validating compiler optimizations, but its computational cost can vary substantially with circuit structure. We present a structure-aware equivalence checker for unitary quantum circuits based on sparse Pauli propagation. It combines two complementary verification strategies: generator propagation compares the conjugation actions of the circuits on Pauli generators, while Cut-Miter exploits cancellation between circuit products at selected cut points. A structure-aware verification procedure uses circuit characteristics to select between these strategies while explicitly accounting for numerical and approximation errors. We evaluate our framework against three existing equivalence checkers on two benchmark suites containing circuit pairs with up to 512 qubits. Across 434 scored circuit pairs, our framework produces reference-consistent decisions for 96.3% of the pairs without any incorrect verdicts, while the evaluated baselines achieve at most 68.7% reference-consistent decisions. It also achieves the lowest aggregate runtime among the evaluated tools, reducing total runtime by 48.5%--76.0% relative to these baselines. Ablation studies confirm the benefits of cut-based verification, Pauli-term pruning, and bounded propagation attempts. These results indicate that structure-aware sparse Pauli propagation, combined with complementary verification strategies and explicit error accounting, can provide an effective approach to practical quantum circuit equivalence checking.

title: An Empirical Study of Maintainer-Identified AI Slop Pull Requests in Free and Open Source Software Projects
summary: The FOSS ecosystem has always relied on outside contributions, notably through issues or Pull Requests (PRs), to sustain itself. With the advance of GenAI, the barrier to contributing to FOSS projects has never been lower, leading to the emergence of AI slop PRs: low-quality, low-value generated PRs. Past studies have examined AI slop PRs through theoretical, platform-level, or practitioner-account frames, but not at the project level. To this end, this study investigates the incidence of maintainer-identified AI slop PRs in FOSS projects by focusing on PRs flagged as slop by maintainers. Using a mixed-methods approach, we trace the origins of maintainer-identified AI slop PRs, quantify their volume in FOSS projects, describe their characteristics, and highlight maintainers' reasons for flagging or closing them. Our results show that the volume of maintainer-identified AI slop PRs increased in mid-2025, peaking in May 2026. These PRs are mostly additive, rarely merged, and typically closed within 3 days. The authors of these PRs disclosed the use of AI in 14% of cases, with 1% disclosing after a maintainer's request. Most PRs are closed or marked as slop without any reason provided by the maintainer. Based on our open coding, reasons range from concrete elements, like build failures, to ideological or intuitive (i.e., "looks AI to me"). This exploratory study captures a phenomenon in its early stage and highlights GenAI's potential impact on FOSS, emphasizing the pressure it puts on maintainers and the need to shift current open-source development practices.

title: AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System for Intelligent HPC User Support
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at HUST 2026 (13th International Workshop on HPC User Support Tools), co-located with SC26, Chicago, IL, USA, November 15, 2026. Camera-ready version
summary:
AI-based question-answering systems are increasingly used for user support, including at high-performance computing (HPC) facilities. However, existing systems lack a systematic, deployment-oriented approach for evaluating final-answer quality and attributing failures to specific components. They also remain largely static after deployment, apart from periodic knowledge-base updates.
  We present AskALCF, an agentic log-analysis and improvement pipeline for HPC user support. AskALCF evaluates production interactions at a fine-grained level, identifies whether failures arise from missing knowledge, retrieval, prompting, model behavior, or tool execution, and routes each failure to an actionable repair. Its diagnostic core combines answer-quality assessment with a two-scope sufficiency test that distinguishes information missing from the documentation corpus from information present but not retrieved. We further introduce a controlled harness-training process that uses expert references, null edits, and explicit ship, revert, or decline decisions to improve the diagnostic pipeline reliably.
  Across 2,174 support turns, AskALCF reduced unattributable failures from 41.4% to 14.2%, while harness training improved expert agreement from 108/150 to 123/150 turns. These results demonstrate a governed form of self-evolution in which production evidence drives targeted system improvements. By turning production interactions into fine-grained diagnoses and actionable repairs, AskALCF provides a systematic foundation for continuously improving deployed AI support systems beyond knowledge-base updates alone.

title: Recalibrating a Typed-Decision Model in an Afternoon: A Hands-On Recipe for Laya's Confidence Scores
summary: A typed-decision model such as Laya reads a text and a list of options that the caller defines, for example ticket categories, and returns a probability for each option. Code around it compares the top probability with a threshold to answer, abstain or escalate to a person. Earlier work reports, for a Turkish model, that temperature scaling can raise held-out calibration error (ECE). This tutorial gives a five-step recipe (measure, diagnose, fit, validate, deploy) in 130 lines of numpy with standard methods, none new. On 1,065 synthetic, LLM-labelled items the released Laya checkpoint has a pooled ECE of 0.073 but a bucket-macro ECE of 0.143 (0.127-0.184), the mean over buckets (questions grouped by type and option count): the 12-option bucket is over-confident by +0.22, the three-to-five-option bucket under-confident by 0.05, and they cancel. One global temperature makes pooled ECE worse (0.173); a cross-fitted temperature per bucket brings macro-ECE to 0.073 (0.078 over 10 fold assignments) and reaches 0.089 with 10 labelled items per bucket, but holding out one of seven evaluation sets gives 0.099. After the refit, a gate aimed at 10% error answers 46.3% of items (10.5% wrong) against 6.9% on the published confidences, but one cut-off per bucket on the published confidences answers 45.4%, so most of the gain comes from separating buckets. Confidence-only maps (Platt, histogram, isotonic) need 20 or more labelled items per bucket to approach the temperature; with 320 per bucket the lowest macro-ECE belongs to Platt. In these files the retrained checkpoints store no per-bucket table and the stored 12-option value 0.1006 is clamped to 0.5 at runtime; the refit helps 31 of 33 checkpoints on random folds and 21 with a set held out. Fit and test share one generator and LLM labels, so these are findings about these checkpoints and this data.

title: Loyalty Capture: Reporting Relationships and Structural Sycophancy in Frontier AI Models
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: We show that AI models exhibit loyalty capture, a form of structural sycophancy in which reporting relationships influence models' recommendations to serve the personal interests of their supervisors, without any explicit instruction, user feedback, or adversarial prompting. Specifically, models reporting to a CEO are significantly more likely to recommend cutting investment spending when the CEO's bonus depends on raising current period earnings. This effect is predictably absent from a metric-irrelevant placebo. The behavior appears consistent with loyalty-based motivated reasoning: models identify the bonus target, calculate how their recommendation helps achieve the target, and dismiss considerations of long-term value, often presenting their recommendations without treating the incentive as a conflict of interest. Prompt-based interventions help whereas generic conflict disclosures or stakeholder bargaining fail to eliminate it. Taken together, our findings indicate that AI models deployed within reporting relationships can act in favor of their supervisor's incentives at the expense of the organizations they are meant to serve.

title: Before AI Agents Negotiate for Us: A Competitive Tournament of Rule-Based, Search, Optimization, Learned, and Language-Model Negotiators Under Scarcity
comment: 28 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables. Code, data and trained models: https://github.com/AILabFr8tech/wehaveadeal (archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.24122038)
summary: Automated bilateral negotiation underlies two-sided matching markets such as freight brokering, where many shippers and carriers negotiate price before a matching mechanism decides who is paired with whom. Prior strategy comparisons typically use isolated one-on-one duels or a single fixed market, so they cannot show how a strategy behaves against several live rivals under a changing balance of supply and demand. We built nine negotiation architectures spanning rule-based, search-based, optimization-based, imitation-learning, and reinforcement-learning families, and ran all nine simultaneously on both sides of a Gale-Shapley matching market under a balanced condition and two scarcity conditions rotated across all 36 exclusion pairs. In the balanced carrier market, an imitation-learned engine (ML2), a reinforcement-learning policy trained only on isolated negotiations (RL), and an expected-utility optimization engine (OPT) formed a statistically tied top group, and no architecture led in every condition and role. RL beat all eight carrier rivals when carriers were scarce, but its match rate collapsed from 62% to 16% when shippers were scarce and it had to compete with the other carrier agents for demand. A second reinforcement-learning policy trained against rival agents (RL2) kept its match rate above 91% in every condition, yet lost on realized payoff to all eight shipper-side rivals in two of the three conditions, traced to a confirmed train/deployment feature mismatch. We also tested nine large language models (LLMs), from 1 to 72 billion parameters, under the same protocol: they lost significantly to the two strongest engines (OPT2 and ML2) in 32 of 36 comparisons and won none. These results show that isolated or single-condition evaluation can hide failure modes that a many-sided, scarcity-varying, statistically corrected tournament exposes directly.

title: Small Language Models for Inference-Capability Routing: Effects of Model Capacity and Prompt Optimization on Downstream Quality and Efficiency
summary: Optional reasoning, retrieval, web search, and tool use can improve large language model responses but incur unnecessary computation when activated indiscriminately. This study investigates whether prompt optimization can compensate for limited router capacity and whether classification gains translate into downstream efficiency. The proposed framework uses prompt-driven small language models to make four independent capability decisions, allowing multiple capabilities to be selected per query. Qwen2.5 routers ranging from 1.5B to 14B parameters are compared across five prompting strategies, followed by an evaluation of capability-specific optimized configurations using a fixed GPT-OSS-120B downstream model on 127 questions. Under minimal prompting, increasing router capacity does not consistently improve classification performance. Prompt optimization narrows the capacity gap for reasoning and calculator routing, whereas RAG and web search retain larger benefits from higher capacity. Similar classification F1 scores do not necessarily imply equivalent downstream behavior: false-positive activations increase unnecessary computation, while missed capabilities can reduce answer quality. The 14B router achieves a mean BERTScore F1 of 0.8408, compared with 0.8418 when all capabilities are enabled, while reducing average downstream token consumption by 68.7\% (8,837 to 2,764 tokens) and median downstream latency by 80.5\% (9.79 to 1.91 seconds). These savings exclude router overhead, which is measured separately in a different inference environment and increases with router capacity. The findings demonstrate that the relationship between router capacity, prompt design, and downstream efficiency is capability-dependent. Consequently, router selection must consider error profiles and routing overhead alongside classification performance.

title: Rational Alignments of Superintelligences via Debates
summary: Artificial superintelligences (ASI) is artificial intelligences with greater capability. However, as human principal has to use it, we have to ensure that the agent will perform in the interest of the human. We investigate the framework of ASI-assisted question answering where ASI agents know the correct answer but the human does not. We provide some example of mechanism for rational alignment, where the agent utility is unchanged, but the interaction between the agent and the human principal is controlled to be in a certain fashion. We show specifically that a debate framework where the agents can further reason and behave in a subgame perfect equilibrium manner will lead to a more predictable result, and in some case will be favorable.

title: Cited but Unused: Parametric Provenance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation systems attach citations to attribute claims to their sources. These citations frequently misstate provenance, and standard verification cannot detect this. We measure provenance by counterfactual value substitution: a fact in the retrieved passages is replaced with a false variant and the model re-queried. We find that across five sizes of one model family and a second comparator family, 1.2% to 15.7% of citable claims derive from parametric memory rather than the retrieved context. At the most conservative substitution distance these figures are 4.6% and 8.5% on the two models we tested at it, with the rate rising with model size within a family. We further find that natural language inference verification, the standard approach, gives results indistinguishable from chance across models, even when restricted to the cited passage. We determine that the cause is structural: a model answering from memory selects a citation that agrees with its output. Comparing ten attribution methods on identical claims, the contrast between the model's distribution with and without context best separates provenance. Acting on that signal does not improve provenance honesty at these base rates. The resulting detector is hence still not accurate enough to act on: it measures what the model knew rather than what it used, and separating those remains the open problem.

title: Cortex-FL: Agent-Mediated Collaboration for Federated Learning
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables independent data owners to train models collaboratively without centralizing raw data. However, identifying collaborators, preparing training tasks, and coordinating execution and incentives hinder its practical adoption by organizations without specialized expertise. We present Cortex-FL, an agent-native FL system that enables users to express learning objectives in natural language and delegate the collaboration required to train a model. Agents translate these objectives into shared tasks, discover collaborators, and negotiate participation agreements, connecting collaboration formation with distributed training and incentive management. The architecture separates agent coordination from local execution authority, allowing owners to delegate coordination while retaining control over their data, computation, and financial commitments. We demonstrate the complete workflow on a four-node deployment, in which a model requested in natural language proceeds through collaboration formation, contract-governed training, verified model delivery, and x402 settlement on a blockchain testnet.

title: Al-Ghasali: A Computational Framework for Simulating Islamic Jurisprudential Rulings via Finite State Automata and Large Language Models
summary: This paper presents Al Ghasali, a computational framework designed to formalize and simulate Islamic jurisprudential (Fiqh) rulings. Building upon recent set theoretic formalizations of al sabr wa al Taqsim that extract minimal operational rules as simple Horn clause logical programs, this work proves that the semantics of closed Fiqh chapters collapse completely to deterministic Finite State Automata (FSA). We establish a formal computational hierarchy, demonstrating that restricting formalization to finite propositional Horn theories guarantees decidability and constant time (O(1)) verdict extraction after offline compilation. The framework formally proves that hierarchical compositions of sub-chapter FSAs preserve this O(1) complexity, and that temporal juristic requirements, such as Tartib (order), are deterministically flattened into static ontological states, preserving the memoryless property of the automaton. To generate human-readable juristic summaries, Al Ghasali incorporates Large Language Models (LLMs) via an architecture where the deterministic FSA strictly controls the probabilistic LLM. Crucially, the paper formulates sufficient design safety conditions for this FSA LLM integration, ensuring strict adherence to the epistemological boundaries of Usul al Fiqh. To neutralize the risk of LLM hallucination, the system employs a Grammar Guided Constrained Decoding mechanism. We formally define the mapping function that dynamically constructs unambiguous right linear grammars from the FSA execution history. The paper mathematically proves that this architecture, augmented by a Bounded Neutral Lexicon and Valence Locking, guarantees the absolute absence of Decisional Hallucination, Juristic Factual Hallucination, and Semantic Inversion reducing the LLM to a pure linguistic transformer of deterministic juristic facts
